description: A vertical jump today against your rested best: this test shows where you are standing on your own curve right now. Here is why the curve, not the muscle, is the program, and how five years of well-timed ordinary sessions outbuild every heroic plan.

scenes.narration: Today's test takes ten seconds and a wall. Stand beside it, reach up and mark your highest touch standing. Then jump, from a quick dip, no run-up, and mark your highest touch again. The difference between the marks, in centimeters, is your jump, and it is the purest power reading your body gives without equipment. Now the context that makes it today's subject: note how long it has been since your last hard leg session, in hours, and write it beside the jump. If you have a rested jump recorded from earlier in this series, write that too. A jump is a nervous system event wearing a leg costume: it needs fuel, freshness and recruitment all present at once, which makes it the perfect single probe for where you currently stand on your own recovery curve.

beats.text: ENTHUSIASM IS NOT ON THE COMMITTEE

scenes.label: YOUR RESTED JUMP IS THE CURVE'S SUMMIT MARKER
scenes.narration: Here is how to read today's probe. A jump at ninety-five percent or better of your rested best means you are standing on the rise or the summit itself: every system the jump consults has been repaid, and a hard session scheduled today would be launched from the platform progress is built on. Eighty-five to ninety-five is mid-curve, the honest middle of the journey, fine for technical and moderate work. Under eighty-five percent, the jump reports a dip still in progress, whatever your enthusiasm says, and enthusiasm, as this season has established, is not on the committee. The rested best matters because it converts a raw jump into a position, and position is the only thing a schedule has ever needed. You are not measuring how high you jump today. You are measuring where today lives.
scenes.sub: today at 95%+: on the rise - 85 to 95%: mid-curve - under 85%: still in the dip

scenes.narration: Step back and look at what the curve really is, because this is the season's thesis and it deserves one clean statement. Training does not make you stronger. Training makes you tired in a very specific, productive way, and then recovery, given fuel, sleep and time, rebuilds you slightly past where you started. The muscle is the site of the work, but the curve is the shape of the becoming, and every result you have ever gotten arrived riding it. This is why the curve matters more than muscle in the only sense that counts for planning: two men with identical muscles and different schedules diverge completely within a season, because one keeps landing on his rises and the other keeps spending from his dips. The mirror photographs muscle. The calendar decides what the muscle becomes. Your jump today is the calendar, reporting in centimeters.

The long-horizon evidence is where the curve stops being a model and becomes a verdict on careers. Studies of training frequency and periodization keep finding the same pattern from different angles: distributing the same total work so that hard efforts land on recovered systems beats compressing it, across months, by margins that dwarf most supplement effects ever measured. Meanwhile the detraining research draws the curve's far side: the overshoot, unvisited, decays back to baseline within roughly the same span it took to build, which is why consistency is not a virtue in this system but a mechanism. Miss the rise and the rise leaves. Put the two findings together and the season's mathematics is complete: progress equals the sum of overshoots actually caught, nothing else, and catching them is a scheduling skill that any man can learn with a wall, a clock and a notebook.

Let me make the stakes concrete with two imaginary trainees, both you, across one year. The first trains by mood: huge sessions when motivation strikes, long gaps when it does not, max tests attempted at random hours of random curves. His year contains perhaps forty genuine overshoot landings, scattered between dips he trained through and rises he slept past. The second trains by the curve: moderate sessions, surveyed spacing, tests only when the jump probe says the rise is near. His year contains over a hundred landings, none heroic, each adding its small overshoot to the last. They did similar total work. They do not finish in similar places, and the difference was never effort, talent or muscle. It was arithmetic: a hundred small rises compound; forty scattered ones mostly cancel. This is the deepest sense in which the curve matters more than the muscle it builds. The muscle is the balance. The curve is the interest rate.

The skinny man's advantages converge in this episode like rivers. Your dips are shallower, so your curves complete faster and your year holds more landings. Your tests are free and instant, a wall and ten seconds, so you can probe your position before every important session instead of guessing, a luxury no gym schedule sells. Your training load is your body, identical daily, so the probe's readings compare across months with laboratory cleanliness. And your whole system, training, testing, recovering, happens inside one life with no facilities between you and the work, which means the schedule the science demands is a schedule you can actually keep for five years. The heavy, busy, gym-bound man must negotiate with the world to ride his rises. You need a wall and a decision. Over five years, that difference is not a convenience. It is the result itself.

Now we practice the summit skill. Five rounds: fifteen seconds of maximum jumps, full intent, then forty-five seconds of rest. When jump height visibly fades, the round ends early: we train the rise, not the dip.

The curve protocol, the season's closing prescription, four rules. One: probe before you spend: a quick jump, hang or max set check before hard sessions, and the honesty to demote the session when the probe says dip. Two: schedule from your surveyed curves, each system on its own clock, the week built in shifts, exactly as the corrected method drew it. Three: prefer the moderate session you can repeat on the rise over the heroic one that buys a canyon, every time the choice appears, for the rest of your training life. Four: retest the jump monthly against your rested best and log the percentage beside the hours since hard work, so your curve stays surveyed as you change. You are not a man who trains and hopes anymore. You are a man who lands on rises, on purpose, in writing.

beats.text: THE SUM OF THE CURVES YOU RODE

scenes.narration: So, your verdict, and the season's. A jump at ninety-five percent or better today: you are standing on the rise, and whatever you train today is being built on the only ground that compounds. Eighty-five to ninety-five: mid-curve, the working middle, where technical volume belongs and where patience is a training variable. Under eighty-five: the dip is still speaking, and the strongest available move is to listen, train light, and let the curve finish its sentence. In every band the thesis holds: your recovery curves matter more than your muscle, because the muscle is only ever the sum of the curves you rode to build it. Put your jump in the comments, just the number. In thirty days, we measure where you stand again.

Thirty days from now, same wall, same two marks, hours since hard work written beside them. Bring me a higher jump and a position you chose on purpose. Subscribe, and keep today's marks safe until then. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: Why Your recovery curves Matter More Than Muscle (The supercompensation Episode)
